reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent claims from multiple distinct sites covering discovery, physical oddities, and the core mystery of its acceleration.
story: In October 2017, astronomers in Hawaii discovered a visitor unlike anything ever seen: 1I/ʻOumuamua, the first known object from another star system. This 400-meter-long 'messenger' was reddish, shaped like a giant cigar, and tumbling through space. As it headed away from the Sun, it did something impossible for a simple rock: it sped up. Usually, only comets do this by venting gas, yet ʻOumuamua had no visible tail, dust, or coma. This 'ghost' acceleration sparked wild theories, from nitrogen icebergs to an artificial alien light sail. While most scientists now believe it is a natural 'dark comet' venting invisible hydrogen, the true nature of this interstellar guest remains one of the greatest riddles in modern astronomy. Because it was already leaving the solar system when discovered, we may never know for certain what it was.
angle: A 400-meter-long interstellar visitor shaped like a giant cigar sped up as it left our solar system without a visible tail, leading some scientists to suggest it was an alien spacecraft.

claims.claim: ʻOumuamua is the first confirmed interstellar object detected passing through the Solar System.
The object was discovered on October 19, 2017, by the Pan-STARRS telescope in Hawaii.
Its name, ʻOumuamua, is Hawaiian for 'scout' or 'messenger from afar arriving first'.
The object has a distinct reddish color, likely from millions of years of exposure to cosmic rays.
It is highly elongated, with a length estimated at roughly 400 meters (one-quarter mile).
Observations indicate its length-to-width ratio is approximately 10 to 1.
ʻOumuamua showed no signs of a coma, dust cloud, or tail, even when closest to the Sun.
The object exhibited non-gravitational acceleration, speeding up as it moved away from the Sun.
Its trajectory was hyperbolic, meaning it is not bound to the Sun and will leave the Solar System.
It entered the Solar System from the approximate direction of the star Vega.
The brightness of the object varied by a factor of 10 as it moved.
The International Astronomical Union created a new designation 'I' for interstellar objects specifically for it.
Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb proposed the object could be an artificial light sail from another civilization.
The Green Bank Telescope searched for radio signals from the object but found none.
A 2023 theory suggests the acceleration was caused by invisible hydrogen gas venting from water ice.

disputed: Specific shape: While many sources describe it as cigar-shaped with a 10:1 ratio, S1 notes that some light curve models suggest it could be a flat, disc-like object.
Tumbling vs. Spinning: S1 specifies the motion is 'tumbling' rather than 'spinning,' while S2 refers to it 'spinning on its axis.' The script should use 'tumbling' to emphasize the unusual motion.
Composition: Sources vary between describing it as dense rock and metal (S2, S7) versus potentially being made of exotic hydrogen or nitrogen ice (S1, S4, S5).
Alien origin: This is presented as a controversial hypothesis by Avi Loeb rather than a scientific consensus; the script must attribute this to specific theorists.
